site.welcome: hi, i'm grace, a designer and curious overthinker. click around to explore what i'm thinking and learning about in my digital garden.
site.about:
A digital garden is a personal website for collecting ideas and thoughts. It's closer to a notebook or a journal than a blog: nothing here is finished, and most of it is still changing. It's also a way of thinking in public without performing! With the increasing pressures of social media, I've come to realize that having a space to myself is cathartic, in a way.

Instead of a feed, the garden is organized by connection. Every thought is filed next to the ones it's related to, and the topics grow out of the thoughts rather than the other way around. You're meant to wander: follow a nearby thought, follow another, end up somewhere you didn't mean to go.

thoughts.text:
Sociopath, a memoir...I initially came across this book because of this video by the author: 
[https://youtu.be/FTWNnmymMc4]()

Which I have separate thoughts on, but it’s interesting and worth watching! Especially the comments.

Overall thoughts:

I’ve always been fascinated by AS#PD, mostly because I enjoy fictional villains. Reading this book, however, forced me to confront my own biases and realize I have strict preconceived notions about how a “normal” person acts.

Initially, I was unsympathetic to Patric’s plight, but towards the end I could understand her a bit more. I found her voice grating and her constant deflection, “technically, it wasn’t a crime”, exhausting. I saw her go through the same destructive cycle over and over. For example, her breaking into houses and defending the act by reasoning, “nobody was home, blah blah, and it’s not like anyone was hurt,” read like a strained justification. She knows it’s bad but tries to rationalize it, which is a common human deflection.

To her credit, she does explain herself: because she wouldn’t care if someone did that to her, there is no barrier to her doing that to someone else. It is the absence of key emotions that enables her actions: shame, guilt, and empathy are the things that hold the rest of us in an invisible contract. However, because the author forces the reader to read between the lines to understand her self-deception, I’m not sure this book would actually land as a helpful or authentic guide for other sociopaths who may not be at the same level of awareness she supposedly is.

This book constantly wonders what it means to be a “good” person. Patric references her destructive tendencies as her “dark side” (lowkey cringe but ok) and clearly grapples with it. Since there is no universal scale for goodness, I found the documentation of her struggle deeply valuable. Upon reflection, I knew that if she had not been labeled a sociopath, I would have extended more nuance and empathy to her desire for change. It is that conscious effort, Patric understanding her need for it and actively working to undo her destructive coping mechanisms, that I found genuinely impressive. Doing right by others is hard work when it doesn’t come naturally, and that is a truth that applies universally.

Other thoughts:

- The fact that she grew up in privilege affects literally everything about her life experience. Her wealth and social standing likely dictated how often she got away with her destructive behavior and enabled her access to the resources needed for eventual change. I don’t remember this mentioned at all in the book, which is weird because she does mention that sociopathy is most likely a combination of environmental and biological factors.
    
- The entire memoir feels incredibly self-congratulatory. Her partner alleges she is a “trailblazer,” but I struggle to see what she has done to improve the view of sociopaths. Normalizing sociopathy feels dangerous to me, though I admit that might be my own bias.
    
- Are we skipping the fact that her dad is implied to be a predator and she didn’t turn him in? Her excuse was that she “doesn’t know right from wrong,” but…girl, lmfao. 
    
- I caught myself thinking I couldn’t trust the book because she’s a sociopath. But to be honest you can’t trust any memoirist. Everyone edits their life to look better.
    
- The epilogue contains a bit about her complaining about how people don’t extend empathy to sociopaths because they’re humans like everyone else. I suppose that’s one way to put it, however empathy requires a certain amount of expectation for reciprocation before it becomes something else more nefarious. I am not saying to treat sociopaths badly, but she’s said it herself: she doesn’t understand or care about kindness and “niceness”, so it reads like she just wants a pass for acting poorly. Her lack of understanding for that is prevalent throughout the book.
    

Beyond the narrative content, the book’s structure was frustrating. I hated the constant flashbacks and the forced time-skips used to accommodate them. They felt unnecessary and poorly executed, often disrupting the emotional momentum. While I understand that this disjointed presentation could theoretically mimic the way a person with ASPD might withhold information or lie by omission, the device felt less like an intentional artistic choice and more like a poorly constructed timeline or just a way to include shock factor when she decided to mention something traumatic she’d inflicted on another person. Ultimately, it just made the listening experience tired and tedious.

Ultimately, this book is about a woman struggling to understand herself in the context of “normal” society. It is an undeniably privileged and self-congratulatory memoir, yet to me it was still fascinating. Even if you question the validity of her diagnosis, the underlying struggles (masking, fitting in, and grappling with the desire to be “better”) are more universal. I’m glad she found a path that works for her, but I would never want to meet her.
thoughts.title: Thoughts on Patric Gagne's memoir Sociopath

A syllabus for understanding yourself

The overall philosophy
- Journal and document your life—experiences, feelings, memories, and things you find beautiful or meaningful.
- When you're obsessed with something, research it deeply: its history, symbolism, origins, context, etc.
- The idea is that by investigating why you're drawn to something, you'll often discover something about yourself.
- The creator also suggests an optional creative project: make a film or cinematic vlog about yourself and your life.
Week 1: Find your myth and your symbol
Study Greek mythology and find a myth that genuinely resonates with you or feels representative of your life/personality.

Then:
- Research different versions and interpretations of the myth.
- Ask yourself why this particular story resonates with you.
- Find a flower that represents you and deeply research its symbolism rather than choosing one based on an obvious cliché.
The example used is Narcissus and Echo, with the daffodil representing themes connected to transformation, death, rebirth, reflection, and self-discovery. The point isn't really the flower itself—it's practicing the ability to connect external symbols to your internal identity.    Pasted text(1)
Week 2: Create an “orbital journal”
Take your abstract interests, obsessions, feelings, and drives and turn them into something physical and visible.

Create a small book filled with things in your “orbit,” such as:
- Pictures
- Quotes
- Words and definitions
- Objects and imagery
- Art and branding
- Strange facts
- People or expressions
- Things you find beautiful, disturbing, sad, fascinating, etc.
It doesn't need to be traditionally written like a diary. It's more like a physical collection of everything that keeps appearing around your mind and interests.

The idea is that once you collect these things together, patterns may emerge and you may look at the finished collection and think: “Oh—that's me.”    Pasted text(1)
Week 3: Abandon yourself temporarily
After spending two weeks intensely focusing on yourself, the third week is about stepping away from your constructed identity.

Suggestions include:
- Wear simple, neutral clothing.
- Don't focus much on appearance, makeup, mirrors, or aesthetics.
- Focus on basic daily life and getting out of your own head.
- Volunteer or physically help someone, ideally doing hands-on work that makes you focus outward.
At the end of the week, write three versions of yourself as three different characters in the third person—as if someone else were observing you.

The purpose is to see yourself from outside your own perspective, including qualities you might not normally acknowledge. It's about recognizing that you don't completely control how you're perceived and giving yourself a fresh perspective on your identity.    Pasted text(1)
Week 4: Free association
Record yourself talking freely for around 40 minutes.

The instructions are essentially:
- Lie down somewhere comfortable.
- Start with how you're feeling that day.
- Don't make an outline.
- Don't script anything.
- Let one thought lead to another.
- Record it, then listen back afterward.
The goal is to see where your mind naturally goes when you're not carefully controlling your narrative. The creator sees recording yourself as a tool that can be used for genuine introspection rather than just performance or social media.    Pasted text(1)
The main takeaway
The video's core argument is that no one is inherently boring or without depth. People become “surface level” when they don't investigate their own experiences, interests, contradictions, and patterns.

The goal of the syllabus is essentially:
Look closely at what you love, what you repeatedly return to, what fascinates you, and how other people see you—then use all of that to build a deeper understanding of who you actually are.

It's less about finding one neat label for yourself and more about collecting evidence of yourself until patterns begin to emerge.
thoughts.title: A four-week syllabus for understanding yourself

Journal prompts for when nothing is going your way

Some weeks are heavier than others. You start focusing so much on what’s not working, what’s delayed, uncomfortable, uncertain, or disappointing, that your mind slowly begins filtering your entire life through frustration.

This kind of journaling helps interrupt those spirals.

Not by pretending everything is perfect, but by helping you reconnect with perspective and self-trust again.

These are the prompts I use:
- What is still going right in my life that I’ve stopped noticing?
- What would change if I stopped treating this moment as permanent?
- What have difficult seasons taught me about myself before?
- What is one thing I can still control or improve today?
- What would it look like to believe things could still work out for me?

Sometimes the most important mindset shift is remembering that a difficult moment is not the same thing as a doomed future.
thoughts.title: Journal prompts for when nothing is going your way

How to inspire without consuming content
1. go on a walk and let your thoughts wander
2. write a page about "things i'll probably forget"
3. write down thoughts before they fully form let them stay messy and unfinished
4. pick a random object in your room and imagine its "backstory"
5. create something that has no purpose, no use, no outcome

link.title:
Marisa Emillie on Instagram: "I don’t think I’m uninspired. I think I’m just full.
Full of other people’s aesthetics, opinions, versions of “how to be.” Full of answers to questions I never actually asked myself.
And somewhere between scrolling and saving and comparing, I stopped noticing when my own thoughts got quieter.
It’s weird—there’s so much out there, but I feel less like I’m creating and more like I’m remixing lives that aren’t mine.
Maybe inspiration isn’t something I need more of.
Maybe I just need less noise so I can hear myself again.

#creativegirls #findingmyself #romanticizeyourlife #digitaldetox #hotgirlsummer"

5 productivity tips that will change your life, apparently
Choose clarity over productivity 
        1. Have an end goal. Understand the magnitude of what you’re working towards 
        2. What is the ultimate thing you want to achieve? 
        3. Trace decisions towards ultimate goal, 5 year plan, 10 year plan 
        4. Set aside time to think about your goals
2. Maintain a fun no bs routine 
        1. Routine of self care, having fun, being lazy a little bit
        2. Feeding your soul 
        3. Mornings are important 
        4. Stuff like talking walks, naps, frolicking 
3. Write down one new idea a day 
4. Listen to your body 
5. Make a drastic change 
        1. Actively choose the person you want to become and go after it 
        2. Nothing changes if nothing changes
thoughts.title: Five productivity tips that will change your life

Journal prompts for overthinkers
1. what are you trying to recreate every time you fall in love with a song/movie?
2. write about the last time the world briefly regained its color
3. describe the exact kind of attention you've been starving for lately. not "love" 
4. what do you keep trying to "earn". that maybe should've been given freely?
5. if you stopped trying to become "someone interesting," who would you naturally be?
6. when was the last time you felt genuinely calm instead of just distracted? describe the day & events
7. whats the difference between your intruition and your anxiety? explain the moment when you confused one for the other
thoughts.title: Journal prompts for overthinkers
